Revision: Structure and Properties of Cell Membrane
• Cell membrane
• Phospholipid bilayer
• Functions
• Separate intracellular region and extracellular region
• Control substances entering and exiting the cell
• Property
• Selective permeability
• Cell membrane allows some substances to pass in different rates while it restricts certain other substances to pass

Selective permeability of cell membrane
(1)Small non-polar molecules pass the phospholipid bilayer quickly
(2)Polar molecules or ions need to use certain transporter proteins (channel proteins or carrier
proteins) to pass cell membrane
(3)Big molecules (or large amount of substance at the same time) need to form vesicles to pass cell
membrane

Passive Membrane Transport
• Passive transport does not require energy
• “Diffusion
• Substance moves from region of higher concentration to region of lower concentration
• Difference of concentrations (Concentration gradient) determines the rate of diffusion!
• Steeper concentration gradient, Higher diffusion rate

Passive Membrane Transport
• Simple diffusion
• Nonpolar lipid-soluble substances diffuse directly through phospholipid bilayer
• Examples
• Oxygen (O 2 )
• carbon dioxide (CO 2 )
• fat-soluble vitamins
• Ethanol

Passive Membrane Transport
• Facilitated diffusion
• Certain polar water-soluble molecules (e.g. glucose, amino acids, and ions) are transported passively down their concentration gradient by:
• Carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion
• Substances bind to carrier proteins
• E.g. glucose, amino acids
• Channel-mediated facilitated diffusion
• Substances move through channel proteins
• E.g. calcium ions, sodium ions, potassium ions

Passive Membrane Transport • Osmosis • Movement of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from region of higher water potential to region of lower water potential • Water diffuses through cell membranes • Through lipid bilayer • Through specific channel proteins called aquaporins

Active Membrane Transport
• Two major types of active membrane transport methods
• Active transport
• Vesicular transport
• Both require cellular energy to move molecules across plasma membrane for any of these reasons:
• Molecule is too large for channel proteins
• Molecule is not lipid soluble
• Molecule is not able to move down concentration gradient

Active Membrane Transport
• Active Transport
• Requires special carrier proteins (pumps )
• Moves molecules against their concentration gradient (from low to high) ○ This requires energy directly or indirectly ○ Some pumps transport more than one substance
• Antiporters
• transport one substance into cell while transporting a different substance out of cell
• Symporters
• transport two different substances in the same direction

Active Membrane Transport
• Two types of active transport:
• Primary active transport
• Required energy directly
• Secondary active transport
• Required energy indirectly from ionic gradients created by primary active transport

Membrane Transport and Membrane Potential • Selective permeability of cell membrane leads to different concentrations of charged particles in cytoplasm and in extracellular fluid. This results in membrane potential, the difference of voltage across the cell membrane. • In resting state, resting membrane potentials of all human cells range from - 50mV to -100mV, depending on cell type. • negative sign (-) indicates inside of cell is more negative than outside of cell

Membrane Transport and Membrane Potential • Generation and Maintaining of Resting Membrane Potential • (1) Proteins with negative charge are too large and polar. They cannot pass across cell membrane and will be trapped inside cell. • (2) Cell membrane is somehow more permeable to K +. K + are transported out of cells by facilitated diffusion. • (3) Action of Na + /K + pump brings more ions with positive charge out of cell. • Change of membrane potential is very important for the function of mus

Passive Membrane Transport
• Passive transport does not require energy
• “Diffusion
• Substance moves from region of higher concentration to region of lower concentration
• Difference of concentrations (Concentration gradient) determines the rate of diffusion!
• Steeper concentration gradient, Higher diffusion rate

Passive Membrane Transport
• Simple diffusion
• Nonpolar lipid-soluble substances diffuse directly through phospholipid bilayer
• Examples
• Oxygen (O 2 )
• carbon dioxide (CO 2 )
• fat-soluble vitamins
• Ethanol

Passive Membrane Transport
• Facilitated diffusion
• Certain polar water-soluble molecules (e.g. glucose, amino acids, and ions) are transported passively down their concentration gradient by:
• Carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion
• Substances bind to carrier proteins
• E.g. glucose, amino acids
• Channel-mediated facilitated diffusion
• Substances move through channel proteins
• E.g. calcium ions, sodium ions, potassium ions

Passive Membrane Transport
• Osmosis
• Movement of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from region of higher water potential to region of lower water potential
• Water diffuses through cell membranes
• Through lipid bilayer
• Through specific channel proteins called aquaporins

Active Membrane Transport
• Two major types of active membrane transport methods
• Active transport
• Vesicular transport
• Both require cellular energy to move molecules across plasma membrane for any of these reasons:
• Molecule is too large for channel proteins
• Molecule is not lipid soluble
• Molecule is not able to move down concentration gradient

Active Membrane Transport
• Active Transport
• Requires special carrier proteins (pumps )
• Moves molecules against their concentration gradient (from low to high) ○ This requires energy directly or indirectly ○ Some pumps transport more than one substance
• Antiporters
• transport one substance into cell while transporting a different substance out of cell
• Symporters
• transport two different substances in the same direction

Active Membrane Transport
• Two types of active transport:
• Primary active transport
• Required energy directly
• Secondary active transport
• Required energy indirectly from ionic gradients created by primary active transport

Active Membrane Transport
• Two types of active transport:
• Primary active transport
• Required energy directly
• Secondary active transport
• Required energy indirectly from ionic gradients created by primary active transport

Active Membrane Transport
• Two types of active transport:
• Primary active transport
• Required energy directly
• Secondary active transport
• Required energy indirectly from ionic gradients created by primary active transport

Active Membrane Transport
• Important carrier protein in human cells
• Sodium-potassium pump (Na + /K + ATPase)
• Most studied pump
• Pumps 3 Na + out of cell and 2 K + back into cell
• Present in all plasma membranes, but especially active in nerve cells and muscle cells

Active Membrane Transport
• Vesicular Transport (Bulk Transport)
• Involves transport of many molecules, large molecules (E.g. large protein molecules), and fluids across membrane by forming vesicles
• Requires cellular energy
• Vesicular transport processes include:
• Endocytosis: transport into cell
• Exocytosis: transport out of cell

Active Membrane Transport
• Vesicular Transport (Bulk Transport)
• Involves transport of many molecules, large molecules (E.g. large protein molecules), and fluids across membrane by forming vesicles
• Requires cellular energy
• Vesicular transport processes include:
• Endocytosis: transport into cell
• Exocytosis: transport out of cell

Active Membrane Transport
• Endocytosis
• Involves formation of vesicles by invagination of cell membrane to transport certain substance into cytoplasm
• Example: Phagocytosis
• The cell engulfs a large particle by enclosing it within a vesicle called a phagosome. The phagosome is then combined with a lysosome.

Active Membrane Transport
• Exocytosis
• Process where material is ejected from cell by secretory vesicle
• Secretory vesicle contains the molecules. The vesicle fuses with cell membrane and release the molecules to outside of cell. ○ Examples ■ hormones, neurotransmitters, mucus, cellular wastes

Membrane Transport and Membrane Potential
• Selective permeability of cell membrane leads to different concentrations of charged particles in cytoplasm and in extracellular fluid. This results in membrane potential, the difference of voltage across the cell membrane.
• In resting state, resting membrane potentials of all human cells range from - 50mV to -100mV, depending on cell type.
• negative sign (-) indicates inside of cell is more negative than outside of cell

• In resting state, resting membrane potentials of all human cells range from - 50mV to -100mV, depending on cell type.

Membrane Transport and Membrane Potential
• Generation and Maintaining of Resting Membrane Potential
• (1) Proteins with negative charge are too large and polar. They cannot pass across cell membrane and will be trapped inside cell.
• (2) Cell membrane is somehow more permeable to K +. K + are transported out of cells by facilitated diffusion.
• (3) Action of Na + /K + pump brings more ions with positive charge out of cell.
• Change of membrane potential is very important for the function of mus

quotation_candidates.quotation: • Revision: Structure and Properties of Cell Membrane
• Membrane Transport and Membrane Potential
• Separate intracellular region and extracellular region
• Control substances entering and exiting the cell
• Cell membrane allows some substances to pass in different rates while it restricts certain other substances to pass
Selective permeability of cell membrane
(1)Small non-polar molecules pass the phospholipid bilayer quickly
(2)Polar molecules or ions need to use certain transporter proteins (channel proteins or carrier
(3)Big molecules (or large amount of substance at the same time) need to form vesicles to pass cell
• Substances move through the cell
membrane by 2 types of methods:
do not consume cellular energy
cellular energy is consumed directly or
• Passive transport does not require energy
• Substance moves from region of higher concentration to region of lower concentration
• Difference of concentrations (Concentration gradient) determines the rate of diffusion!
• Steeper concentration gradient, Higher diffusion rate
• Nonpolar lipid-soluble substances diffuse directly through phospholipid bilayer
• Certain polar water-soluble molecules (e.g. glucose, amino acids, and ions) are transported passively down their concentration gradient by:
• Carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion
• Substances bind to carrier proteins
• Channel-mediated facilitated diffusion
• Substances move through channel proteins
• E.g. calcium ions, sodium ions, potassium ions
• Movement of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from region of higher water potential to region of lower water potential
• Water diffuses through cell membranes
• Through specific channel proteins called aquaporins
• Ability of a solution to change the shape of cells by altering the cells’ internal water volume
• Isotonic solution has same tonicity as inside the cell, so volume of cell remains unchanged
• Hypertonic solution has higher osmolarity than inside cell, so water flows out of cell, resulting in cell shrinking
• Hypotonic solution has lower osmolarity than inside cell, so water flows into cell, resulting in cell swelling or bursting
• Two major types of active membrane transport methods
• Both require cellular energy to move molecules across plasma membrane for any of these reasons:
• Molecule is too large for channel proteins
• Molecule is not able to move down concentration gradient
• Requires special carrier proteins (pumps )
• Moves molecules against their concentration gradient (from low to high) ○ This requires energy directly or indirectly ○ Some pumps transport more than one substance
• transport one substance into cell while transporting a different substance out of cell
• transport two different substances in the same direction
• Two types of active transport:
• Required energy indirectly from ionic gradients created by primary active transport
• Important carrier protein in human cells
• Sodium-potassium pump (Na + /K + ATPase)
• Pumps 3 Na + out of cell and 2 K + back into cell
• Present in all plasma membranes, but especially active in nerve cells and muscle cells
• Vesicular Transport (Bulk Transport)
• Involves transport of many molecules, large molecules (E.g. large protein molecules), and fluids across membrane by forming vesicles
• Vesicular transport processes include:
• Endocytosis: transport into cell
• Exocytosis: transport out of cell
• Involves formation of vesicles by invagination of cell membrane to transport certain substance into cytoplasm
• The cell engulfs a large particle by enclosing it within a vesicle called a phagosome. The phagosome is then combined with a lysosome.
• Process where material is ejected from cell by secretory vesicle
• Secretory vesicle contains the molecules. The vesicle fuses with cell membrane and release the molecules to outside of cell. ○ Examples ■ hormones, neurotransmitters, mucus, cellular wastes

• Selective permeability of cell membrane leads to different concentrations of charged particles in cytoplasm and in extracellular fluid. This results in membrane potential, the difference of voltage across the cell membrane.
• In resting state, resting membrane potentials of all human cells range from - 50mV to -100mV, depending on cell type.
• negative sign (-) indicates inside of cell is more negative than outside of cell
• Generation and Maintaining of Resting Membrane Potential
• (1) Proteins with negative charge are too large and polar. They cannot pass across cell membrane and will be trapped inside cell.
• (2) Cell membrane is somehow more permeable to K +. K + are transported out of cells by facilitated diffusion.
• (3) Action of Na + /K + pump brings more ions with positive charge out of cell.
• Change of membrane potential is very important for the function of muscular system and nervous system.
